editorial.tldr: This is a loose cluster of arXiv papers that share the word "optimization", not one developing story; it was reclustered away from the earlier multi-agent grouping. It now holds two research strands: agent RL and preference-optimization recipes (TSBPO, DNO, steerable multi-objective GRPO, PORT), and agents that optimize GPU kernels and AI infrastructure (question-driven kernel agents, a local 7B model study, Infrathon).
editorial.whats_new: Nov 13: AscendGYM added a cost-aware kernel-optimization benchmark for real workloads on Ascend NPUs, and VEPO proposed preference optimization grounded in visual evidence to cut multilingual hallucination in vision-language models.
editorial.why_it_matters: Kernel and infra tuning is becoming a benchmarked agent task, and preference optimization is being adapted for noisy labels and shifting objectives; every result here is author-reported on the papers' own benchmarks, not production evidence.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you trial an agent for kernel or infra tuning, gate every change on a correctness check before measuring speed, and compare against your current vendor-library baseline; treat the preference-optimization results as candidates for your own eval, not drop-in replacements for DPO.

beats.headline: Small-model routing tries to switch on reasoning, retrieval and tools only when a request needs them

open_questions: Does any independent group reproduce TSBPO's gains on long-horizon agent tasks outside the paper's own environments?
Do kernel-optimization agents beat vendor libraries and hand-tuned kernels on Infrathon or AscendGYM workloads under their cost accounting?
Can a locally hosted 7B code model produce correct CUDA kernels reliably enough to use without a larger model in the loop?
Does PORT's token-level reweighting hold its advantage when preference-label noise is measured on real production feedback?
Does small-model routing cut compute without a measurable quality drop on traffic other than the study's benchmark?
